paragraphs: §1 — What reached Q of Qūmisī's denial of the angels: the angels as calamities, and the angels as created for the moment
I have not ascertained his statement on this matter — how it stands, nor what compelled him to it, nor with what he argues for it — save that there reached me concerning him, of that, two statements.

The first of them: that he alleges that the angels (al-malāʾika) are only the afflictions and the calamity (al-āfāt wa-l-balwā) which God (mighty and exalted) sends upon people; and I suppose he argued for that from the saying of Scripture [Ps 78:49] יְשַׁלַּח בָּם חֲרוֹן אַפּוֹ עֶבְרָה וָזַעַם וְצָרָה ("He sent against them His burning anger, wrath, indignation, and trouble"), then it says מִשְׁלַחַת מַלְאֲכֵי רָעִים ("a deputation of angels of evil"). And the like of that, in [holding] that the fire and the wind are the angels, arguing from the saying of Scripture [Ps 104:4] עֹשֶׂה מַלְאָכָיו רוּחוֹת מְשָׁרְתָיו אֵשׁ לֹהֵט ("who makes the winds His messengers, the flaming fire His ministers"). And of this same kind is His saying [Exod 13:21] וַה' הֹלֵךְ לִפְנֵיהֶם יוֹמָם בְּעַמּוּד עָנָן ("and the Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud"); and it says [Exod 14:19] וַיִּסַּע מַלְאַךְ הָאֱלֹהִים הַהֹלֵךְ לִפְנֵי מַחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל ("and the angel of God who went before the camp of Israel set out"), then it says [Exod 14:19] וַיִּסַּע עַמּוּד הֶעָנָן מִפְּנֵיהֶם וַיַּעֲמֹד מֵאַחֲרֵיהֶם ("and the pillar of cloud set out from before them and stood behind them"). So this, in his view, indicates that the two pillars — of fire and of cloud — were named מַלְאָךְ ("angel"); and this is recorded in his books.

: The first reported doctrine: angels are not subsistent beings but a way of speaking of the natural/providential instruments by which God acts — calamities (Ps 78:49, where malʾakhei raʿim, "angels of evil," is read as a deputation of disasters), and the elemental fire and wind (Ps 104:4) and the pillar of cloud and fire of the Exodus (Exod 13:21; 14:19), where "angel" and "pillar" are used interchangeably of the same phenomenon. The reduction is naturalistic-figurative: malʾakh names the effect, not an agent. Q's hedge — "I have not ascertained his statement… save that there reached me" — is honest source-criticism; he is working from report (and Qūmisī's books) rather than direct refutation, a caution he repeats at §4 about the line of transmission.
§1 (continued) — The second report: the angels created for the moment of their appearance

And the second statement that reached me concerning him is that he alleges, regarding the individuals (al-ashkhāṣ) named among them — namely that the prophets saw them in the form of men and addressed them, such as גַּבְרִיאֵל (Gabriel) and others — he says that they were created [only] for their moment (makhlūqīn li-waqtihim), just as the garments that were seen upon them were created [only] for their moment; since it was, in his view, of the impossible that they should be in the highest abode (al-maḥall al-aʿlā) wearing garments — and if the garments seen upon them were created only for their moment, it must follow that they too were created only for their moment.
: The manuscript marks a note-pointer "(1)" here; the referent is not preserved in the OCR. Rendered as written.

: The second reported doctrine concerns the named, anthropomorphic angels (Gabriel, etc.) who appear to prophets in human form. Qūmisī (as reported) makes these ad hoc creations — brought into being for the instant of the apparition and then ceasing — by analogy with the clothing they were seen wearing: since (he reasons) it is absurd that beings of "the highest abode" should be permanently clad in garments, the garments must be momentary creations; and if so, then the angels wearing them must be momentary creations too. The argument trades on the indignity of supposing celestial beings to be permanently garbed. Q will answer it in §4 by pressing the consequences for the angels' speech and tasks (an angel created only for the moment could not promise Jacob, or announce a return "next year," etc.).
§2 — The consensus of Israel, and the witness of Scripture, refute the doctrine

And the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the house of Israel, from the beginning of the world to its end, invalidates this statement; for not one of them has dissented regarding the angels — [holding] that they are living, speaking individuals (ashkhāṣ aḥyāʾ nuṭuq), created together with the creation of the world, whose abode is in the heavens, glorifying their Creator (mighty and exalted) and praising Him. And the reports of Scripture necessitate that in many places — among them the saying of Jacob [Gen 48:16] הַמַּלְאָךְ הַגֹּאֵל אֹתִי ("the angel who redeemed me"); and among them what יְחֶזְקֵאל (peace be upon him) reported of what he saw of the four living creatures (אַרְבַּע חַיּוֹת) and the form of the wheels (al-awfān) and their shapes and their figures, and likewise the cherubim (הַכְּרוּבִים); and the saying of יְשַׁעְיָהוּ [Isa 6:2] שְׂרָפִים עֹמְדִים מִמַּעַל לוֹ ("seraphim standing above Him"), and his saying [Isa 6:3] וּקְרָא זֶה אֶל זֶה וְאָמַר ("and one called to another and said"), and his saying [Isa 6:6] וַיָּעָף אֵלַי אֶחָד מִן הַשְּׂרָפִים ("then one of the seraphim flew to me"); and likewise what דָּנִיֵּאל reported in his saying [Dan 7:10] אֶלֶף אַלְפִים יְשַׁמְּשׁוּנֵהּ וְרִבּוֹ רִבְבָן קֳדָמוֹהִי יְקוּמוּן ("a thousand thousands served Him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before Him").

: al-awfān (الأوفان) renders Ezekiel's אופנים ("wheels," Ezek 1:15-21; 10) — the Hebrew term carried over into the Arabic. Read with the cherubim (Ezek 10) and the four living creatures (ḥayyot, Ezek 1) as the standard repertoire of Ezekiel's chariot-vision angelology.

: The positive scriptural case for angels as permanent, living, rational individuals "created with the creation of the world" and dwelling in the heavens in perpetual praise. Q's prooftexts cover the patriarchal "redeeming angel" (Gen 48:16), Ezekiel's merkavah beings (the four ḥayyot, the wheels, the cherubim), Isaiah's standing-and-calling seraphim (Isa 6:2-6), and Daniel's myriads who "serve" and "stand before" God (Dan 7:10) — the last decisive because the angels there serve continuously, which is incompatible with momentary creation. Note the appeal to ijmāʿ ("consensus of the house of Israel from the beginning of the world to its end"): Q meets an intra-Karaite dissenter (Qūmisī, a founding Karaite authority) with the same consensus-plus-Scripture weaponry he turns elsewhere on Christians and on the resurrection-deniers (cf. Bab 8 §2) — angelology is here treated as a matter of settled communal doctrine, not open naẓar.
§3 — The "angels of evil" usage does not generalize; even a human may be called malʾakh

And it is not [the case] that, since the afflictions and the calamity have been named in the Torah לֹא חָמָס מַלְאַךְ רָעִים, it must follow that whenever a deliverance is [effected], "angel" must be its description — since the human being too may be named מַלְאָךְ ("messenger").

: The Hebrew here is garbled in the manuscript and the reference is uncertain; the run as transmitted (לֹא חָמָס מַלְאַךְ רָעִים) appears to conflate the malʾakhei raʿim of Ps 78:49 (cited in §1) with another phrase. The sense Q draws on is secure: that Scripture's occasional use of malʾakh for an impersonal "messenger of evil" does not license the general inference that all angels are mere calamities. Flagged for the edition.

: The logical core of the answer to the first doctrine (§1): the occasional metaphorical use of malʾakh — for calamities (Ps 78:49) or for a human emissary (the standard sense of malʾakh = "messenger," e.g. human envoys throughout the historical books) — does not warrant the universal claim that angels are only such things. From "some X are called malʾakh" one cannot infer "all malʾakh are X." The point that a human being too is called malʾakh is doubly apt: it shows the word's range is wide, so no single referent (calamity) can be read into every occurrence.
§4 — The angels created for the moment cannot do what Scripture says angels do; and Q's surmise about Qūmisī's motive

And how is it admissible to say that the angels were created [only] for their moment — which is the moment of the need to dispatch them — and that they are cut off [thereafter], together with the saying of the angel [Gen 32:27] וַיֹּאמֶר שַׁלְּחֵנִי כִּי עָלָה הַשָּׁחַר ("and he said: let me go, for the dawn has risen")? For if that for which [the angel] was created — namely a purpose (wajh) in it — had already elapsed, and his being cut off had become obligatory, then what is the meaning of his asking of Jacob that he release him? And how is that admissible, together with the saying of דָּנִיֵּאל [Dan 9:21] וְהָאִישׁ גַּבְרִיאֵל אֲשֶׁר רָאִיתִי בֶחָזוֹן בַּתְּחִלָּה ("and the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the first"), and the saying of יְחֶזְקֵאל (peace be upon him) in the second vision [Ezek 10:20] הִיא הַחַיָּה אֲשֶׁר רָאִיתִי תַחַת אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּנְהַר כְּבָר ("it was the living creature that I had seen beneath the God of Israel by the river Chebar") etc.? And the matter in this is plainer than that we should need to be prolix about it. And firmer than that, or the like of it, is the saying of the angel to Abraham [Gen 18:14] לַמּוֹעֵד אָשׁוּב אֵלֶיךָ כָּעֵת חַיָּה ("at the appointed time I will return to you, at the season of life") etc. — for one who is cut off, how does he return after a year? And the like of that is the saying of Manoah to God [Judg 13:8] אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר שָׁלַחְתָּ יָבוֹא נָא עוֹד אֵלֵינוּ וְיוֹרֵנוּ ("let the man of God whom You sent come again to us and instruct us").

And I do not suppose that what carried Daniel al-Qūmisī (דאניאל הקומסי) to the denial of the angels was anything but what Benjamin [al-Nahāwandī] had shifted to, of the doctrine concerning the angel (al-malāk); and [Qūmisī] wished to declare [God's] unity (yuwaḥḥida) at the root by the single [principle], that he might not affirm any angel at all. And he employs the like of this in more than one place.

: Q's refutation of the second doctrine (§1 continued) and his closing surmise. (1) If angels are created only for the instant of their errand and then annihilated, several scriptural narratives become unintelligible: the angel who wrestles Jacob asks to be released "for the dawn has risen" (Gen 32:27) — but why ask release if his purpose (wajh) is spent and he is already due to cease? Gabriel is identified across two separate visions as the same individual "whom I had seen at the first" (Dan 9:21), and Ezekiel's ḥayyah of the second vision is "the [same] living creature I had seen… by the Chebar" (Ezek 10:20) — diachronic re-identification that momentary creatures could not bear. The angel promises Abraham "I will return… at the season of life," i.e. next year (Gen 18:14) — impossible for one "cut off." And Manoah prays that the angel be sent again (Judg 13:8). All four require persisting, re-identifiable angelic individuals. (2) The historical aside: Q surmises that Qūmisī's angel-denial was a reaction against Benjamin al-Nahāwandī's angelology — Benjamin (early-9th-c. Karaite) had given the angel a strong role (in his theology a created angel is the agent of creation and revelation, shielding God's transcendence). Qūmisī, wishing to safeguard divine unity (tawḥīd) "at the root," over-corrected into denying angels altogether — a tendency Q says is characteristic of him ("he employs the like of this in more than one place"). The clause דאניאל הקומסי names the adversary in Hebrew script in the source.

- The bab's subject and adversary. The heading is ʿalayhi fī inkārihi li-l-malāʾika — "On [the refutation of] him regarding his denial of the angels." The pronoun "him" (ʿalayhi) has no antecedent within the bab heading itself; it is supplied by the running structure of this stretch of Maqala III, in which Q refutes Daniel al-Qūmisī (the founding Karaite of the mourners of Zion, fl. late 9th c.) point by point — Bab 21 having defended al-naẓar (rational inquiry) against him, and Bab 23 going on to his view of the age of legal majority. Q names Qūmisī explicitly only at §4 (דאניאל הקומסי). The polemic is thus intra-Karaite, not anti-Christian or anti-Rabbanite — a notable feature: Q is willing to refute a revered Karaite predecessor by name and at length.

- Two doctrines, two refutations. §1 reports two distinct angel-denying positions Q heard attributed to Qūmisī: (a) angels = natural calamities / the elements / the Exodus pillars (a thoroughgoing naturalistic reduction), and (b) the named anthropomorphic angels (Gabriel et al.) = beings created ad hoc for the moment of their appearance and then annihilated. Q answers (a) in §§2-3 (consensus + the prooftext-array + the logical point that occasional metaphor does not generalize) and (b) in §4 (the angels of Scripture persist and are re-identified across time, which momentary creatures could not be).

- Method: ijmāʿ + Scripture, not naẓar. Unlike the rationalist refutations elsewhere in Maqala III, the decisive appeal here is to the consensus of the house of Israel "from the beginning of the world to its end" (§2) plus a dense scriptural florilegium. This is striking given that Bab 21 (just refuted) defended reason against Qūmisī: on the existence and nature of angels Q treats the matter as settled communal-and-scriptural doctrine rather than as an open question for inquiry.

- The Benjamin al-Nahāwandī genealogy (§4). Q's closing surmise is historically valuable: he reads Qūmisī's angel-denial as a reaction against Benjamin al-Nahāwandī's angelology (in which a created angel mediates creation and revelation, protecting divine transcendence). Qūmisī, over-zealous for tawḥīd "at the root," swung to the opposite extreme. This is independent testimony to an inner-Karaite theological debate between two of the movement's founders, mediated by Q in the next generation.

- OCR / citation cruxes. The Hebrew citations in this bab are heavily damaged in the Kraken layer; the merged text follows the multimodal (Gemini) re-OCR, which recovers most of them cleanly (see `diff-report.md`, 65 disagreements, multimodal preferred throughout). Two cruxes remain: (1) the note-pointer "(1)" at §1-continued (referent not preserved — see ); (2) the garbled run at §3, לֹא חָמָס מַלְאַךְ רָעִים (), which appears to be a corrupt echo of Ps 78:49's malʾakhei raʿim and could not be securely resolved. The verse reference for the §4 angel-of-Jacob citation (Gen 32:27, shallḥeni ki ʿalah ha-shaḥar) was reconstructed from the partially-corrupt marginal pointer; Q's own pointer there reads, in the source, as a garbled "דבראש' לְדָנִיֵּאל" — evidently a conflation, since the quoted words are from the Jacob-wrestling narrative, not Daniel. The substantive readings are secure; the marginal sigla are not, and are flagged for the edition.

- For Daniel al-Qūmisī's life, thought, and angelology: Leon Nemoy, "Al-Qirqisānī's Account of the Jewish Sects and Christianity," HUCA 7 (1930); Haggai Ben-Shammai, "The Doctrines of Religious Thought of Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Qirqisānī and Yefet ben ʿEli" (Hebrew diss., Jerusalem 1977); Daniel Frank, Search Scripture Well (2004), on the Qūmisī circle. Qūmisī's own surviving works (the Pitron Shneim ʿAsar commentary on the Minor Prophets, ed. Markon) bear on his exegetical method. - For Benjamin al-Nahāwandī's mediating-angel doctrine (the position Q says Qūmisī reacted against): Nemoy, Karaite Anthology (1952), pp. 21-29; Ben-Shammai on the malʾakh-as-creator/revealer theme in early Karaite theology, and its Philonic/Jewish-gnostic antecedents. - For the angelological prooftexts and the merkavah repertoire (Ezek 1, 10; Isa 6; Dan 7:10): standard commentary; for the Karaite handling specifically, Yefet ben ʿEli ad loc. - For ijmāʿ (consensus) as a source of authority in early Karaism (as deployed in §2): Ben-Shammai and Frank on the tension between naẓar (individual inquiry) and communal consensus in Qirqisānī and his successors. - For Q's broader sequence against Qūmisī in Maqala III (the naẓar defense, B21; the age of legal majority, B23): the anchor-grid for Maqala III, and Q's own programmatic statements in Maqala I on the sects.
